## Why Asked
Interviewers ask this to assess your understanding of DevOps automation and modern CI/CD practices, which are essential skills for software development roles.

## Key Concepts
- Workflows: Automated processes defined in YAML files
- Triggers: Events that start workflows (push, pull request, schedule)
- Jobs: Sets of steps that run on runners
- Actions: Reusable building blocks for workflows
- Runners: Virtual machines that execute workflows

## Code Example
```yaml
name: CI/CD Pipeline
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - name: Run tests
        run: npm test
```

```javascript
- hosts: all
  become: true
  tasks:
    - name: Ensure ops user
      user:
        name: ops
        state: present
        shell: /bin/bash

```

questions.explanation:
Kubernetes supports multiple custom schedulers running alongside the default scheduler through the schedulerName field in pod specifications. When a pod is created with a specific schedulerName, only that scheduler will attempt to place it on a node. The default scheduler ignores pods with non-default scheduler names, while custom schedulers only handle pods matching their assigned name.

Coordination between schedulers occurs through the Kubernetes API server's shared state. All schedulers observe the same cluster state including node resources, existing pod assignments, and taints/tolerations. When a scheduler binds a pod to a node, this information is immediately available to all other schedulers via the API server, preventing double-assignment of resources. Additionally, Kubernetes employs optimistic concurrency control through resource versions to ensure that only one scheduler can successfully bind a pod to a node at any given time.

## Why This Is Asked
This question evaluates your ability to orchestrate multi-tool CI pipelines, enforce reproducible builds, and design fail-safe rollback strategies—skills critical in large organizations with heterogeneous CI ecosystems.

## Key Concepts
- Cross-tool orchestration and unified workflow design
- Immutable artifacts and centralized, versioned manifests

- Health-check-driven rollback mechanisms

## Code Example
```yaml
# Cross-tool correlation ID propagation
# GitHub Actions (PR validation)
env:
  CORRELATION_ID: ${{ github.run_id }}-${{ github.run_attempt }}

# Jenkins (nightly builds)
environment:
  CORRELATION_ID: ${CORRELATION_ID}

# GitLab CI (deployment)
variables:
  CORRELATION_ID: ${CORRELATION_ID}

# Unified rollback endpoint
rollback:
  script:
    - curl -X POST "${ROLLBACK_ENDPOINT}" \
      -H "X-Correlation-ID: ${CORRELATION_ID}" \
      -d "manifest=${PREVIOUS_MANIFEST_SHA}"
```

questions.explanation: Topology spread constraints (introduced in Kubernetes 1.19) provide a declarative way to distribute pods across failure domains like zones, nodes, or custom topology keys. You define constraints using maxSkew (which controls how uneven the distribution can be), topologyKey (the domain to balance across, such as topology.kubernetes.io/zone), and a selector to match pods. The scheduler ensures pods are spread according to these constraints while respecting other scheduling requirements. For example, a deployment with 3 replicas and topologySpreadConstraints set to maxSkew: 1 across zones will distribute replicas across 3 different zones when possible, ensuring no single zone contains more than one additional pod than another. Choose topology spread constraints for simple, uniform distribution across failure domains, and use affinity/anti-affinity when you need complex logic, such asco-locating specific services or spreading based on custom labels beyond standard topology keys.

## Why This Is Asked
Tests the ability to create idempotent, cross-platform automation configurations that handle package manager differences while maintaining consistency across Ubuntu and CentOS systems.

## Key Concepts
- Idempotent package management across Debian and RedHat families

- Git-based application deployment
- Centralized log rotation configuration

## Code Example
```yaml
- hosts: all
  become: true
  tasks:
    - name: Install nginx
      package:
        name: nginx
        state: present

    - name: Ensure nginx service is running and enabled
      service:
        name: nginx
        state: started
        enabled: true

    - name: Deploy website from git repository
      git:
        repo: 'https://github.com/example/website.git'
        dest: /var/www/html
        version: main
        force: true

    - name: Configure log rotation for nginx
      template:
        src: nginx.logrotate.j2
        dest: /etc/logrotate.d/nginx
        owner: root
        group: root
        mode: '0644'
      notify: restart logrotate

  handlers:
    - name: restart logrotate
      service:
        name: logrotate
        state: restarted
```

questions.explanation:
Kubernetes scheduling with affinity and anti-affinity rules follows a hierarchical precedence model to resolve conflicts. The scheduler first evaluates all required rules (hard constraints) across node affinity, pod affinity, and pod anti-affinity. If a pod's required rules cannot be simultaneously satisfied, the pod will remain in a Pending state because required constraints are absolute requirements that cannot be violated.

For preferred rules (soft constraints), Kubernetes employs a scoring mechanism where each preference contributes to a node's overall score. The scheduler weighs these preferences based on their specified weight values (1-100), with higher weights having greater influence on the final placement decision. This scoring approach allows the scheduler to make optimal placement decisions while maintaining flexibility when multiple preferred rules conflict with one another.

questions.explanation:
Kubernetes manages resource contention through pod priority and preemption mechanisms using priority classes, which assign numerical values to pods. When a high-priority pod cannot be scheduled due to insufficient resources, the scheduler identifies and evicts lower-priority pods to free up capacity. This mechanism ensures critical workloads can access resources during contention scenarios. Priority values range from -2 billion to 1 billion, with system-critical pods typically receiving the highest priorities above 1 billion.

However, implementing priority classes requires careful consideration of several factors. Poorly configured priorities can lead to cascading failures where high-priority pods continuously evict lower-priority workloads, creating instability. Resource starvation becomes a concern when lower-priority pods never receive scheduling opportunities. Additionally, excessive preemption can disrupt system performance and impact application availability. Production environments should implement priority classes thoughtfully, with clear guidelines for priority assignment and monitoring to prevent these potential pitfalls.

## Why This Question Is Asked
This assesses practical GitOps implementation skills, specifically the ability to set up Argo CD or Flux in a beginner-friendly manner and demonstrate understanding of environment overlays and drift detection.

## Key Concepts
- **Git as single source of truth**: All desired state lives in Git; the GitOps tool continuously reconciles cluster state to match.
- **Declarative Kubernetes manifests**: Resources are defined as YAML, not imperatively applied.
- **Environment overlays**: Kustomize overlays allow dev/prod to share a base while overriding specific values.
- **Drift detection and reconciliation**: GitOps tools detect when live cluster state diverges from Git state and automatically correct it.
- **Bootstrap workflows**: Initial setup connects the GitOps tool to your cluster and repo.

## Recommended Approach
1. Structure manifests with a `base/` directory for shared configuration and `dev/`/`prod/` overlays for environment-specific overrides.
2. Use Kustomize for lightweight environment management—no additional tooling required.
3. Bootstrap your chosen tool (Flux or Argo CD) directly from the CLI.
4. Verify synchronization using built-in status commands.

## Follow-Up Questions

- What would you do if your cluster drifts from Git state and automatic sync is disabled?
- How would you promote a change from dev to prod using this layout?
- What are the trade-offs between Flux and Argo CD for multi-cluster scenarios?

For production, I'd implement a canary deployment strategy where new features are initially enabled for 1% of users using feature flags, then gradually increase to 10%, 50%, and finally 100% based on monitoring metrics.

The pipeline would include real-time monitoring of key metrics like error rates, response times, and conversion rates. If any metric exceeds predefined thresholds, the pipeline would automatically disable the feature flag and rollback to the previous version. I'd use tools like LaunchDarkly or Unleash for feature flag management, and implement the progressive delivery using Kubernetes with Istio service mesh or AWS CodeDeploy with canary deployments.

The pipeline would also include automated testing of feature flag configurations, ensuring that flags are properly configured and tested before deployment. This approach allows for immediate rollback without requiring a new deployment, and enables A/B testing of new features while maintaining system stability.

questions.explanation:
A GitOps-based CI/CD pipeline treats Git repositories as the single source of truth for both application code and infrastructure definitions. For multi-cluster management, the pipeline should use a GitOps operator (like ArgoCD or Flux) that continuously monitors Git repos and syncs desired state to target clusters. The repository structure typically follows a pattern with separate repos or branches for each environment: `main` for production, `staging` for staging, with each containing environment-specific overlays using tools like Kustomize or Helm values files. The CI pipeline handles testing and building artifacts, then commits manifests to the GitOps repo, triggering the GitOps controller to reconcile state.

Drift detection is critical for maintaining consistency. Implement it using tools like ArgoCD's built-in health assessment, Polaris for configuration validation, or custom controllers like Kyverno that can detect and remediate policy violations. The pipeline should run periodic reconciliation checks (e.g., every 5-15 minutes) comparing actual cluster state against Git state. When drift is detected, create a workflow that: 1) Generates alerts via Slack/PagerDuty for operations teams, 2) Captures the diff showing what changed, 3) Provides options for automatic remediation (for non-critical drift like optional add-ons) or manual approval (for critical changes like security patches or workload modifications).

For the approval workflow, integrate with GitHub/GitLab merge request approvals, requiring sign-off for production changes. Use sealed secrets or external secrets operators (like External Secrets Operator with HashiCorp Vault) to manage sensitive data outside Git. Implement pre-deployment validation gates that check for policy compliance before Git commits are even merged, using OPA/Gatekeeper or Kyverno policies. The pipeline should also maintain an audit trail by logging all sync attempts, drift detections, and remediation actions to a compliance logging system.

To implement a custom Kubernetes scheduler for specialized workloads, you'd start by creating a new scheduler binary that extends the default scheduler framework. The key components include custom Predicates (filtering functions) that can check for GPU availability, memory requirements, and other specialized hardware constraints. You'd also implement custom Priorities (scoring functions) that rank nodes based on factors like GPU model, network bandwidth to storage, or thermal characteristics.

The scheduler would need to be registered with the Kubernetes API server through a scheduler configuration file, and you'd deploy it as a separate pod in the cluster. For GPU workloads specifically, you'd create custom scheduler plugins that interface with the NVIDIA device plugin and can parse GPU-specific annotations and resource requests. You might also implement custom queueing logic to batch ML jobs together for better GPU utilization.

Testing would involve creating node labels for GPU capabilities, deploying test pods with GPU resource requests, and verifying the scheduler places them appropriately. You'd also need to handle edge cases like preemption when high-priority jobs need GPU resources, and implement fallback mechanisms to the default scheduler for non-specialized workloads.

questions.explanation:
The key challenge is creating a unified pipeline that accommodates language diversity while maintaining operational consistency. I'd design a modular pipeline using a repository structure where each microservice has its own language-specific build configuration (package.json, requirements.txt, pom.xml, go.mod) but shares common pipeline templates. The pipeline would use conditional logic to detect the language and trigger appropriate build steps: npm/yarn for Node.js, pip/maven for Python/Java, and go build for Go services. Each service would be containerized using Dockerfiles specific to their language, creating a consistent deployment artifact regardless of the underlying codebase.

For consistency, I'd implement shared quality gates that all services must pass: container image scanning with tools like Trivy, unit test coverage thresholds (using coverage tools appropriate to each language), static code analysis with ESLint/Black/PMD/golint, and security vulnerability scanning. The pipeline would use a matrix strategy to build services in parallel when possible, with dependency management handled through a shared artifact repository. Integration tests would run at the system level, testing service interactions regardless of implementation language.

Deployment would leverage Kubernetes with Helm charts that can deploy any containerized service, using environment-specific values files for configuration. I'd implement language-agnostic monitoring and logging strategies, ensuring all services emit metrics in a standard format. The pipeline would include automated rollback mechanisms and canary deployment capabilities that work across all services, with health checks standardized through Kubernetes probes. This approach allows teams to choose the best language for each service while the platform team maintains operational consistency and governance.
